Product Id: Cancer incidence refers to the number of new cases of primary malignant neoplasms in a population over a given period of time, usually one year. As the CCR is updated annually with new records for current and earlier diagnosis years as well as changes to previous records, the incidence for any given diagnosis year may change from one release to the next. In particular, delays in the reporting of new cases to Statistics Canada typically result in undercounts of cases which are more pronounced in the most recently reported diagnosis year. Generally, the reporting delay ranges between 2% and 3% nationally. The missing cases are added to their appropriate diagnosis year with the reporting of data from a new reference year.

Although the Canadian Cancer Registry (CCR) strives to achieve national uniformity, reporting procedures and completeness vary across the country: a) Differences may exist between the content of the CCR and the provincial and territorial cancer registries. b) Ontario has not yet submitted death certificate only (DCO) cases for 2023 (on average, 1.5% of submitted cancer cases were DCO cases between 2020 and 2022). c) Manitoba has not yet submitted DCO cases between 2013 and 2017 (on average, 0.7% of submitted cancer cases were DCO cases between 2010 and 2012). d) Newfoundland and Labrador did not submit DCO cases before 2006. e) Nova Scotia has not yet submitted DCO cases for 2019 (on average, 2.0% of submitted cancer cases were DCO cases between 2016 and 2018).

Cancer incidence rates are age-standardized using the direct method and the final 2021 Canadian postcensal population structure (opens new window). Age-standardization (opens new window) allows for comparisons of incidence rates over time that are unaffected by changes in the age distribution of the population. The age-standardized rate may be undefined in the event that the underlying population of one or more age groups is 0."

Confidence intervals convey the degree of precision associated with a rate. Wide confidence intervals convey imprecision (that is, high variability) and should be interpreted and compared cautiously. For age-standardized rates, the 95% confidence intervals were calculated using the Poisson distribution for counts greater than or equal to 50 and the method devised by Tiwari, Clegg and Zou (2006) for smaller counts: Tiwari RC, Clegg LX, Zou Z. Efficient interval estimation for age-adjusted cancer rates. Stat Methods Med Res. 2006 Dec;15(6):547-69. doi: 10.1177/0962280206070621. PMID: 17260923.

To prevent inappropriate disclosure of health-related information, the actual number of cases of a specific cancer is randomly rounded to a lower or higher multiple of 5; true zeros and actual counts evenly divisible by 5 are not affected. Random rounding is applied to each cell count independently. Specifically, an unbiased random rounding procedure is applied such that numbers ending in 0 or 5 are not rounded; numbers ending in a 1 or 6 are rounded up with a probability of 0.20 and down with a probability of 0.80; numbers ending in 2 or 7 are rounded up and down with probabilities of 0.40 and 0.60, respectively; numbers ending in 3 or 8 are rounded up and down with probabilities of 0.60 and 0.40, respectively; and, numbers ending in 4 or 9 are rounded up and down with probabilities of 0.80 and 0.20, respectively. Consequently, columns and rows will sum to totals only by chance. By design, differences between the rounded and actual counts will never exceed 4 and actual counts are more likely to be rounded to the nearest multiple of 5. Note that the age-standardized incidence rates and corresponding 95% confidence limits are calculated using the unrounded case counts.

The following standard symbols are used in this Statistics Canada table: (..) for figures not available for a specific reference period, (...) for figures not applicable and (x) for figures suppressed to meet the confidentiality requirements of the Statistics Act.

Nova Scotia cancer incidence data are not available for diagnosis years after 2019. For tables 13-10-0111-01 and 13-10-0747-01, annual case counts and rate estimates for Nova Scotia, Canada and Canada excluding Quebec for the 2020 diagnosis year onward are not provided.

In October 2014, Ontario implemented a new cancer reporting system, the Ontario Cancer Registry. The new system has several enhancements that permit the identification of cancer cases that previously went unrecorded. These include the use of more liberal rules for counting multiple primary sites, the use of additional source records and the inclusion of records that were previously not included. The implementation of this new system affects data from the 2010 diagnosis year onward. Data on in situ carcinomas of the bladder for Ontario were limited to 2010 onward.

The two-sided 95% confidence intervals for average age at diagnosis were calculated based on Student's t distribution. In some instances, when the average age was very young, the lower limit of the confidence interval reached a negative value. For all such cases, the distribution of the mean was left-truncated to zero in order to avoid implausible values.

A national duplicate resolution process covering all data years is typically performed annually to reduce the number of duplicate registered cases in the Canadian Cancer Registry. Using internal record linkage, duplicate patient and tumour records within a province or territory, as well as across provinces and territories, are identified and resolved in consultation with the corresponding jurisdiction(s). However, the process is currently undergoing a review and was not performed for this cycle. The de-duplication process was last completed for all provinces and territories—except Quebec and Nova Scotia—for cases diagnosed up to December 31, 2022. For Nova Scotia, de-duplication was last completed for all cases diagnosed up to December 31, 2019. For Quebec, de-duplication has not yet been completed and is ongoing.
In 2020 and 2021, the registration of new cancer cases in Canada may have been impacted by disruptions in screening and diagnostic services. Therefore, these data should be interpreted with caution.

Product Id: Case ascertainment for Newfoundland and Labrador was substantially improved for the 2006 diagnosis year and onward through the implementation of death clearance processes and the consolidation of information from healthcare organizations by this province.

Cancer incidence rates for both sexes were produced using the total population estimate for both males and females. For sex-specific cancer types (cervix uteri, corpus uteri, uterus, ovary, other female genital system, prostate, testis, penis, and other male genital organs), the rate for both sexes is based on the same count as that of the corresponding sex-specific rate.
